name: Hedy Lamarr
tagline: The Most Beautiful Mind in the Room
story:
In 1942, at the height of her Hollywood fame, Hedy Lamarr sat across from the U.S. Navy's patent office with a sheaf of technical drawings that would have baffled most engineers. She and composer George Antheil had designed a frequency-hopping communication system — a way to make radio-guided torpedoes unjammable by enemy forces. The Navy looked at the glamorous actress, looked at the patent, and filed it away. They told her she'd help the war effort more by selling kisses at bond drives.

Lamarr sold the kisses. She raised $25 million in war bonds in a single night. But she never stopped inventing. In her home workshop, surrounded by drafting tools and engineering manuals she'd taught herself from, she continued refining ideas — an improved traffic light, a tablet that dissolved into a carbonated drink, aeronautic designs she sketched on napkins between film takes. Hollywood called her the most beautiful woman in the world. She wanted to be known as the most interesting.

The frequency-hopping patent gathered dust for two decades until the Cuban Missile Crisis, when the Navy finally implemented her concept in their ships' communication systems. That same technology evolved into the spread-spectrum principles underpinning Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and GPS. Every time you connect to a wireless network, you're using the mathematics of an actress the world refused to take seriously.

She was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2014 — posthumously. She never saw the vindication. But she'd predicted it decades earlier with characteristic sharpness: "Any girl can be glamorous. All you have to do is stand still and look stupid." Hedy Lamarr refused to stand still.
